abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Nemtabrutinib is a Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor under clinical investigation in patients with hematologic malignancies, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL). Nemtabrutinib plasma concentration data from 578 patients enrolled in phase 1 and 2 clinical studies, treated with doses from 5 to 80 mg daily were used to develop a preliminary population pharmacokinetic (PK) model. A two‐compartment model with first‐order absorption with time delay, and first‐order elimination described the data accurately. A full covariate modeling approach was adopted to evaluate prespecified clinically meaningful covariates. The final model included the impact of body weight, sex, race, and disease indication on clearance (CL) and central volume of distribution; age, albumin, moderate CYP3A4 inducers, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, mild hepatic and moderate renal impairment on CL; and acid reducing agents (ARAs) (i.e., proton pump inhibitors, H2 antagonists, and antacids) on bioavailability. The effect of CYP3A4 modulators and ARAs was estimated to be very low (< 4%) and none of the intrinsic factors were found to have a clinically significant impact on nemtabrutinib PK. Preliminary exposure‐efficacy analysis in patients with CLL/SLL showed a significant trend of increased probability of best overall response with increased exposure to nemtabrutinib, while preliminary exposure‐safety in patients with hematologic malignancies showed a significant trend between increased exposure and increased probability of any‐grade drug‐related adverse events (as assessed by investigator) and any‐grade hypertension events. Taken together, these exposure‐response analyses suggest that 65 mg daily is an appropriate dose for nemtabrutinib monotherapy treatment of patients with CLL/SLL.

sec.p: Keywords: exposure‐response, modeling, population pharmacokinetics

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) are the most common adult leukemias in Western countries. Relapsed/refractory disease often occurs due to resistance to prior therapies, including Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitors (BTKi) via BTK mutations at cysteine 481 (C481).

What question did this study address? ○
Nemtabrutinib, an oral, reversible non‐covalent, competitive BTKi that does not require C481 for binding, is in clinical development for hematologic malignancies. The objectives of this study were to develop a population pharmacokinetic (PK) model to assess the impact of intrinsic and extrinsic variables on exposure and analyze exposure‐efficacy and ‐safety relationships for nemtabrutinib in patients with hematologic malignancies.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
A preliminary two‐compartment model with first‐order absorption with time delay and first‐order elimination was developed that accurately captured nemtabrutinib PK upon doses of 5–80 mg. Nemtabrutinib bioavailability was linear at high concentrations, with doses < 30 mg estimated to result in 15% lower relative bioavailability compared to 30–80 mg doses. There were no clinically significant findings that would suggest any need for nemtabrutinib dose adjustments based on covariates tested. Overall, preliminary exposure‐response analyses supported improved benefit‐risk at the phase 2 recommended dose of 65 mg compared to lower or higher doses. The effects of mild hepatic impairment and mild or moderate renal impairment on the PK of nemtabrutinib were not found to be clinically significant.

How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics? ○
No covariates tested suggested any need for nemtabrutinib dose adjustments. The models will be updated with safety and efficacy data from ongoing phase 3 studies and patient‐specific disease characteristics which may impact prognosis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) are the most common adult leukemias in Western countries, with 23,690 new cases and 4460 deaths projected in the US in 2025 [1]. Despite initial high response rates in newly treated patients, relapsed/refractory (R/R) disease due to resistance to prior therapies is common [2].

Inhibitors of cell survival pathways have recently been approved for treatment of patients with CLL/SLL. Specifically, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is critical in the B‐cell receptor signaling pathway that mediates cell growth, adhesion, and survival. First‐generation BTK inhibitor (BTKi) ibrutinib, and next‐generation BTKi acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, are covalent BTKi that have achieved remarkable results in CLL/SLL including in R/R disease [3, 4]. However, resistance to these therapies frequently arises via mutations at BTK cysteine 481 (C481) [5, 6], present in up to approximately 80% of progressive cases [7, 8, 9]. Mutations can disrupt binding of covalent BTKi leading to relapse [7]. Reversible non‐covalent BTKi, such as pirtobrutinib, have emerged as an alternative. However, resistance to non‐covalent BTKi can also occur, and there remains an unmet need for novel BTKi for R/R patients with acquired resistance [10] and frontline options with improved tolerability.

Nemtabrutinib (also known as MK‐1026 and formerly ARQ 531) is an oral reversible non‐covalent adenosine triphosphate competitive inhibitor of BTK that does not require C481 for binding. Its efficacy and safety as monotherapy and in combination with other therapeutic agents are being evaluated in ongoing clinical trials in adults with hematologic malignancies [11]. To date, nemtabrutinib has shown a manageable safety profile, favorable pharmacokinetics (PK), and preliminary efficacy in BTK‐C481 mutant or wild‐type CLL/SLL in the BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 studies [11, 12, 13]. Development of nemtabrutinib as a monotherapy for CLL/SLL is ongoing at the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) of 65 mg daily administered orally.

Nemtabrutinib exhibits good passive permeability, is rapidly absorbed with a median time to maximum plasma concentration (Tmax) of ~2 h, and is eliminated primarily via the hepatobiliary route, with metabolism being a significant elimination pathway. Based on preliminary nemtabrutinib monotherapy PK data from BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003, exposure (area under the concentration time curve from 0 to 24 h [AUC0‐24] and maximum plasma concentrations [Cmax]) generally increased with dose from 5 to 80 mg after both single and multiple nemtabrutinib doses. Mean nemtabrutinib concentrations following multiple daily doses were higher compared to those observed after the first dose, suggesting accumulation of nemtabrutinib. Accumulation ratios ranged between 1.8 to 3.4 for AUC0‐24 and 1.53 and 2.85 for Cmax. Plasma pre‐dose concentrations of nemtabrutinib appeared to reach a plateau after ~15 days over the dose range studied.

The objectives of this research study were to develop a population PK model based on preliminary nemtabrutinib PK data to assess the impact of intrinsic and extrinsic variables, and analyze exposure‐efficacy and ‐safety relationships in patients with hematologic malignancies. The results of these analyses will help inform nemtabrutinib dose selection and dose adjustment in special populations.

sec.title: Data
sec.p: Development of the nemtabrutinib preliminary population PK model was based on data collected in two ongoing clinical studies in patients with hematologic malignancies (Table S1). BELLWAVE‐001 (formerly ARQ 531–101) (NCT03162536) is a phase 1/2 dose escalation study in participants with R/R hematologic malignancies, including CLL/SLL, administering doses from 5 to 75 mg daily in 28‐day cycles. The study aims to evaluate safety, tolerability, and recommended dose regimen of nemtabrutinib monotherapy, as well as PK and pharmacodynamics (PD) and preliminary antitumor activity. In BELLWAVE‐001, treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAE) per investigator assessment led to treatment discontinuation in 14.0% of participants. The most common (> 1% incidence) treatment‐related TEAEs that led to treatment discontinuation were maculopapular rash (2.9%) and platelet count decreased, rash, and hypertension (1.5% each). Study BELLWAVE‐003 (NCT04728893) is a phase 2 dose escalation and confirmation study, followed by a cohort expansion study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of nemtabrutinib in participants with hematologic malignancies including R/R CLL/SLL treated with 45, 65 or 80 mg daily. In BELLWAVE‐003, treatment discontinuation due to treatment‐related TEAEs occurred in 10.3%, 10.8%, and 7.1% of participants in the 45, 65, and 80 mg dose levels, respectively. The most common (> 1 participant) treatment‐related TEAEs that led to treatment discontinuation were hypersensitivity (1.9%) at 80 mg, pneumonia (0.8%) at 65 mg, and an event of arrythmia in 1 patient (7.1%) at 45 mg. Both studies are being conducted in accordance with ethical principles from the Declaration of Helsinki and International Council for Harmonization (ICH) guidelines. The studies were reviewed and approved by an Institutional Review Board. All participants provide informed consent prior to study start.

Intensive and sparse PK samples were collected across both studies (Table S1). Nemtabrutinib plasma concentration was measured using a validated liquid chromatography assay coupled with tandem mass spectrometric detection with a lower limit of quantification of 1 ng/mL and an upper limit of quantification of 1000 ng/mL. Participants who received ≥ 1 nemtabrutinib dose and had ≥ 1 measurable nemtabrutinib plasma concentration were considered evaluable and retained in the PK analysis population.

sec.title: Population PK Modeling
sec.p: The population PK analysis was performed using a non‐linear mixed effect (NLME) modeling approach in NONMEM, v7.5.1 (ICON Development Solutions, Ellicott City, MD, USA), supported by PsN version 5.3.1 (psn.sourceforge.net). R v4.3.3 (R‐project, www.r‐project.org) was used for data visualization and post‐processing of NONMEM output. Observations with missing time or date or with missing dosing information were excluded from the analysis. A total of 4% of all post‐dose observed concentrations were below the limit of quantification (BLQ) and were excluded from analysis. Two trough concentrations that were unrealistically high were also excluded from the analysis.

sec.title: Structural and Stochastic Model
sec.p: For the structural model, one, two, and three compartment models with linear absorption and elimination were tested. Inclusion of inter‐individual variability (IIV) on model parameters was tested on all structural parameters assuming a log‐normal distribution. For the residual error structure, an additive, proportional, and combined error model was tested. For model selection, a drop in objective function value (OFV, −2 log‐likelihood) was considered statistically significant if p < 0.05. Assuming a χ 2 distribution, this corresponds to a drop of more than 3.84 points between nested models with a difference of 1 degree of freedom. Additionally, standard goodness‐of‐fit (GoF) plots were visually assessed for improvements in the fit.

sec.title: Covariate Analysis
sec.p: A full covariate modeling approach [14] was adopted to evaluate the impact of selected continuous and categorical covariates that were chosen a priori based on their anticipated relevance for nemtabrutinib PK. In this approach, all prespecified covariates are retained in the final model regardless of estimated effect size or precision. Unlike stepwise covariate selection, this approach avoids selecting amongst correlated covariates based on repeated p‐value based assessments without multiplicity corrections. While certain covariates were correlated (See Figures S1 and S2 and Supporting Information), it was deemed plausible that > 1 of these correlated covariates could be independent predictors of exposure variability; for instance, body weight (organ size) and race (genetics) could have independent effects on clearance (CL). Therefore, covariate analysis was not restricted to uncorrelated covariates. However, as a consequence of this approach, coefficients could not be uniquely identified for each covariate effect. The clinical significance of covariates was instead assessed via post hoc simulations preserving correlation structure between covariates.

Since body weight was assumed to be an important mechanistic covariate, which could not be identified as such when it was included in the full covariate modeling approach, power functions based on body weight were estimated first for CL and central distribution volume (Vc) as part of initial covariate model development. The obtained coefficients were fixed in the subsequent fit with the full covariate model. Body weight was highly correlated with race, sex, disease indication, and renal impairment (Figure S1), and the potential additional effect of these correlated covariates was subsequently studied during full model development. The full model included body weight on CL and Vc; sex, race, and disease indication on CL and Vc; age, albumin, moderate CYP3A4 inducers, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and hepatic and renal impairment on CL; and acid reducing agents (ARAs) (i.e., proton pump inhibitors, H2 antagonists, and antacids) on bioavailability (F). A comprehensive list of covariates including their detailed descriptions and derivation methods is provided in Table S2.

The population characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Continuous and categorical covariates were modeled based on log‐linear and linear relationships, respectively. Covariates were only considered in the analysis if values were available in at least 80% of the included participants. Missing continuous covariates were imputed with the median values and missing categorical covariates were merged with the largest category. Categories of categorical covariates were only included if ≥ 10 of participants were available in that category; otherwise, they were merged with the largest category. For race, “other” was merged with “White.” For disease indication, “other” was modeled as a separate category.

sec.p: The effect of CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers, and ARAs was considered only when there were records of concomitant administration with nemtabrutinib (Table S3). Consequently, these extrinsic factors were treated as time‐dependent regressors.

sec.title: Model Evaluation
sec.p: For model evaluation, visual inspection was performed of the standard GoF plots, including observed (DV) versus individual (IPRED) and population (PRED) predictions, conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) versus time since first dose, time since last dose, and PRED. Plots were stratified by dosing regimen. Visual predictive checks (VPCs), based on 500 simulations, were used to evaluate the predictive ability of the final model.

sec.title: Assessment of Covariate Effects
sec.p: The potential impact and relevance of covariate effects were assessed by evaluating the estimated covariate effect size as well as the estimated relative standard error of the estimates, the latter of which expresses the certainty of the obtained estimates. However, because of correlations amongst covariates, absolute values of covariate effect estimates should be interpreted with caution. The clinical significance of the impact of intrinsic covariates on nemtabrutinib exposure was instead evaluated by simulations. Forest plots were generated using the coveffectsplots package in R. For this, individual (i.e., post hoc) PK profiles were simulated using each participant's actual dosing history and individual parameter estimates. For every simulated concentration sample, the value was normalized by the dose administered immediately before that sample (i.e., the last dose preceding the time point). From these dose‐normalized concentration‐time profiles, the exposure metric was then calculated as cumulative AUC over the entire treatment period divided by the time on treatment (Cavg). Variations in Cavg within and between subgroups were visually compared. For continuous covariates, the comparison was obtained by splitting the data into quartiles and the range of values corresponding to the third quartile was used as a reference. For categorical covariates, normal hepatic function, normal renal function, CLL/SLL, and White were used as a reference for the typical individual.

sec.title: Exposure‐Response Analyses
sec.p: The exposure‐efficacy and exposure‐safety analyses were based on individual exposure metrics that considered individual specific dosing history, including potential dose interruptions or dose adjustments, and time‐varying covariates. Cavg (defined as the cumulative on‐treatment AUC divided by the treatment duration) and Cmax, calculated as maximum concentration reached throughout treatment, derived from simulations with the final model based on individual post hoc PK parameter estimates, were investigated for correlations with efficacy and safety endpoints. The primary efficacy endpoint was the best overall response (BOR). Responders were defined as those patients who attained a partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) at any time throughout the treatment and time on therapy was evaluated as a covariate. For patients who dropped out of the study, we assessed whether or not they attained PR or CR, while their exposure was calculated based on the time they remained in the study. The exposure‐efficacy analysis included data from all participants included in the population PK model who had a primary diagnosis of CLL/SLL and who completed at least one treatment cycle with nemtabrutinib.

Safety endpoints, selected prior to the analysis based on their severity and the frequency with which they were experienced by patients with hematologic malignancies, included neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, infection, rash, hemorrhage, hypertension, diarrhea, and arrhythmia. Additionally, tolerability endpoints including dose interruption, reduction, discontinuation, and dose‐limiting toxicity were evaluated. Time on treatment was also investigated as a covariate for the safety endpoints. The exposure‐safety analysis included data from all patients who were part of the population PK analysis.

Multivariate logistic regression was used to study the association between exposure and BOR or safety endpoints and time on treatment. Within the logistic regression model (logit function), exposure was treated as a linear predictor of response, whereas time on treatment was considered as a saturable sigmoidal predictor. This parameterization was adopted because the effect of time on response rate is only expected to persist initially. Improved response rates or deepened responses with continuous therapy over longer time have in fact been shown for nemtabrutinib and other BTKi [15, 16]. The proportion of responders rises rapidly in the first 3–6 months of BTKi treatment and more slowly through ~12 months, after which rates of CR may still improve, but new responses become less common [16, 17].

sec.title: Data
sec.p: This population PK analysis was based on 5669 non‐BLQ observations from 578 participants, including both intensive and sparse sampling upon administration of nemtabrutinib doses between 5 and 80 mg. Table 1 provides an overview of the characteristics of the included participants. Patients within this population and with available safety and PK data were included in the exposure‐safety analysis (N = 578). The exposure‐efficacy analysis was performed only on the largest subset of patients, namely those patients with a CLL/SLL diagnosis and available response and PK data (N = 288).

sec.title: Population PK Modeling
sec.p: The PK of nemtabrutinib was best described by a two‐compartment model with first‐order absorption with time delay, and first‐order elimination. IIV was included on CL and Vc, and a combined proportional and additive error structure was used to describe random unexplained variability. As non‐linearities were observed in F for doses < 30 mg (Figure S3), a fractional deviation in F was estimated for these low doses.

The impact of body weight on CL and Vc was quantified with a power function, estimated to be 0.331 and 0.807, respectively. These values were fixed in the subsequent fit of the full covariate model. The final parameter estimates obtained in the full model are presented in Table 2. The estimated apparent clearance in a typical participant was 3.33 L/h and the volume of distribution from the central compartment was 120 L. The terminal half‐life of nemtabrutinib derived from the obtained parameter values was 85 h.

sec.p: The structural model parameter values and those related to the stochastic model (e.g., IIV and residual unexplained variability) could generally be estimated with good precision, as the percent relative standard error (RSE) was generally well below 50% and the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the estimates did not include zero. Estimates of the covariate effects were generally obtained with higher imprecision, with RSE values above 50% and/or 95% CI ranges that included zero, suggesting that values could not be estimated with a high degree of certainty.

The full model attained reduced IIV on key PK parameters compared to the base model. IIV on CL decreased from 48.0% to 39.8% and IIV on Vc decreased from 27.5% to 17.1%, indicating that inclusion of additional covariates helped better explain between‐subject variability. Eta‐shrinkage was below 20% for both parameters. The residual variability was similar between models. The parameter estimates for the final model are shown in Table 2.

GoF plots and VPCs of the full model are provided in Figures S4 and S5, respectively. These plots show good descriptive and predictive model performance with unbiased prediction of both high and low concentrations and doses without bias over time.

sec.title: Assessment of Covariate Effects
sec.p: The forest plots illustrating the impact of intrinsic covariates on nemtabrutinib Cavg are shown in Figure 1. Forest plots illustrating covariate effects on CL and Vc at baseline are shown in Figures S6 and S7, respectively. Trends were found for some covariates, including younger age and lower albumin levels which were both correlated with lower exposure, and lower body weight, female sex, and Asian race which were correlated with increased exposure. However, the geometric mean ratio (GMR) for the effect of each covariate on Cavg was within bioequivalence bounds of [0.8, 1.25], suggesting that each covariate had limited influence on nemtabrutinib exposure. Doses < 45 mg (approximately 30% lower than 65 mg) had lower efficacy, and those > 80 mg (approximately 25% higher than 65 mg) had unacceptable toxicity based on initial clinical data from BELLWAVE‐003. Thus, bioequivalence bounds of [0.8–1.25] were considered relevant for clinical activity as well.

Missing continuous covariates were imputed with the median values, and missing categorical covariates or categories with insufficient participant numbers (n < 10) were merged with the largest category. For race, “other” was merged with “white;” for disease indication, “other” was modeled as a separate category. Blue circles represent the GMR, the blue bars indicate the 90% CI. sec.p: The estimated effect of CYP3A4 comedications on CL/F was very low (< 3%) and could not be reliably estimated, as indicated by RSE values above 50% and the fact that the 95% CI included zero (Table 2). The frequency of nemtabrutinib observations while the participant was on concomitant treatment with moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers was very small (Table S3), suggesting limited interpretability of the effect of CYP3A4 inhibition and induction on nemtabrutinib exposure.

Patients were enrolled in BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 studies without restricting their concomitant use of ARAs, which allowed for the accrual of considerable clinical data on the impact of ARAs on nemtabrutinib F and exposure (Table 1 and Table S3). ARAs used by patients while on treatment with nemtabrutinib included antacids (e.g., calcium carbonate, magnesium carbonate), proton pump inhibitors (e.g., esomeprazole, pantoprazole) and histamine H2 receptor antagonists (e.g., famotidine, cimetidine), which were each treated as individual covariates in the full model. Based on these data, the impact of ARAs on nemtabrutinib F was estimated to be very low (< 4%), with considerable uncertainty of these estimates.

sec.title: Model Derived Individual Exposure Metrics
sec.p: The population PK model was used to calculate average and maximum concentrations for each participant in the analysis. The applied calculations accounted for individual dosing history and for individual‐specific PK parameter values.

Figure 2 depicts the individual average (Cavg) and maximum concentrations (Cmax) of nemtabrutinib for each dose grouped by study. The distribution of individual concentration values and the overlayed error bars show wide variability across dose levels with a general trend of increasing individual concentration with increasing dose across studies. Cavg and Cmax based on the population PK model were significantly correlated and Cavg was used as a predictor of safety, tolerability, and efficacy as well as in simulations of the impact of intrinsic factors on nemtabrutinib exposure as presented in the following sections.

The triangle and error bar indicate mean concentration ± standard deviation. BW‐001, BELLWAVE‐001 study; BW‐003, BELLWAVE‐003 study; n, number of participants.

sec.title: Exposure‐Response Analyses
sec.p: The relationships between exposure, Cavg, follow‐up time, and BOR defined as PR or CR were assessed by multivariate logistic regression in CLL/SLL patients across studies BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003. The parameter estimates from the final exposure‐response model are provided in Table S4. The results of this analysis are depicted in Figure 3. The observed exposure distributions for nemtabrutinib monotherapy at doses of 45, 65, and 80 mg, which are the doses received by most patients, are shown for reference at the bottom of the exposure‐response/safety plots. A significant trend was observed between exposure and probability of BOR and between time on treatment and BOR (Figure 3), both being included as continuous variables. To visualize this relationship, two simulated treatment durations are shown at 180 days and 360 days, with the latter leading to higher response rates. This is consistent with clinical evidence for nemtabrutinib, as well as other BTKi, showing improved response rates or deepened responses with continuous therapy over a longer time [15, 16].

caption.p: Exposure‐efficacy analysis of BOR vs. nemtabrutinib concentration in CLL/SLL. The red, blue, and green horizontal boxplots depict the distribution of nemtabrutinib exposure at 45, 65, and 80 mg respectively. Edges of the box indicate the 25th/75th percentile, and whiskers refer to the smallest and largest values within 1.5 times the interquartile range above/below the 75th/25th percentile. Similar reference boxplots are also shown for exposure‐safety figures. Shaded areas indicate the 95% confidence interval of the regression. The orange solid line and shaded area refer to a simulated treatment time of 180 days; the brown solid line and shaded area refer to a simulated treatment time of 360 days. BOR, best overall response; Cavg, average nemtabrutinib concentration (ng/mL) over treatment duration; CLL/SLL, chronic lymphocytic leukemia and small lymphocytic lymphoma.

sec.p: All patients in our current analysis had received prior treatment, and many of them had missing TP53 gene mutation status. Thus, while prior lines of treatment and mutational status are covariates expected to be relevant predictors of efficacy, they could not be evaluated in this analysis. Univariate logistic regression was also conducted to assess the relationship between BOR and exposure to nemtabrutinib. Figure S8 shows the predictions overlaid with the observed data.

The relationship between safety and exposure to nemtabrutinib when administered as monotherapy in studies BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 was evaluated in all treated participants regardless of their primary diagnosis (N = 578). Figure 4 shows that a trend was found between nemtabrutinib Cavg and any‐grade drug‐related adverse events (AEs) (as assessed by the investigator) and between nemtabrutinib Cavg and any‐grade hypertension. Time on therapy was not found to be a significant covariate for these exposure‐safety relationships. Importantly, no trend was found between exposure and Grade 3+ drug‐related AEs or between exposure and Grade 3+ hypertension. Additional selected safety endpoints including any grade and Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, infection, arrhythmia, diarrhea, rash, and hemorrhage were considered in the analysis because of their possible relevance to the patient population, and no trend was found between exposure and the occurrence of such events. Tolerability of nemtabrutinib as monotherapy was evaluated by analyzing preliminary data on patients' individual dosing history. No trend was found between tolerability endpoints, including dose interruption, reduction, discontinuation, dose‐limiting toxicity, and exposure to nemtabrutinib monotherapy.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: A preliminary population PK model was developed that accurately captured the nemtabrutinib PK profile across doses from 5 to 80 mg. The model was based on pooled data from phase 1/2 and phase 2 studies enrolling 578 oncology patients with hematologic malignancies including CLL/SLL. The model described data across studies, doses, and disease indications well. The most suitable structural model was a two‐compartment model with first‐order absorption with time delay, and first‐order elimination. Nemtabrutinib F was linear at high concentrations, but doses < 30 mg were estimated to result in 15% lower relative F compared to doses from 30 to 80 mg.

An exploratory analysis of the intrinsic and extrinsic population characteristics revealed extensive correlation amongst several potentially clinically meaningful covariates that were planned to be evaluated. A full model approach was therefore used, as it considers any relationships found between selected clinical covariates and exposure equally plausible and avoids any biased decision making that a covariate search methodology would inherently require [14, 18, 19, 20]. However, given that body weight was correlated with most other covariates and given the prevalence and mechanistic plausibility of this covariate for CL and Vc, we estimated body weight relationships first and fixed the obtained parameter values in the full covariate model. After the inclusion of covariate relationships that indicated an increase in CL and Vc with body weight, the full covariate model described a decrease in CL with age, albumin, sex, Asian race, and B‐Cell non‐Hodgkin lymphomas; a decrease in Vc with sex and Asian race; and an increase in Vc in patients with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. However, given the correlations, the clinical significance of these findings was based on simulations rather than the absolute values of each individual covariate estimate. The analysis did not indicate any clinically significant findings that would suggest dose adjustments are warranted based on these covariates.

Nemtabrutinib is eliminated primarily via the hepatobiliary route, with metabolism being a significant elimination pathway, with only minimal (~3%) renal excretion. Patients with moderate and severe hepatic impairment and with severe renal impairment are currently excluded from enrolling in nemtabrutinib clinical trials, while the impact of organ impairment on nemtabrutinib exposure is being investigated in two ongoing, dedicated clinical pharmacology studies. In our analysis, while mild renal impairment did not result in any clinically meaningful change in exposure, patients with moderate renal impairment were found to have increased exposures. Given the low contribution of renal excretion to the overall elimination of nemtabrutinib, this could be the result of differential representation of other correlated covariates in this population (Figures S1 and S2). Specifically, patients with renal impairment were more likely to be older with lower body weight and albumin. Overall, based on the data accrued so far and this population PK analysis, the effects of mild hepatic impairment and mild or moderate renal impairment on the PK of nemtabrutinib are not clinically significant.

Nemtabrutinib exhibits pH‐dependent solubility and meets regulatory agency recommendations [21] for assessing the potential for drug interactions with ARAs, which by elevating the gastric pH could alter nemtabrutinib solubility, dissolution, and F. Given that early preliminary clinical PK data did not show evidence that would suggest a clinical significance of nemtabrutinib in vitro pH‐dependent solubility, patients were enrolled in BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 studies without restricting their concomitant use of ARA. The preliminary results of our analysis estimated that the use of ARAs resulted in a minimal < 4% change in F, which is not expected to translate to a meaningful exposure change or require a dose adjustment for patients on ARAs (Table 2).

Based on the favorable benefit–risk profile demonstrated in BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 studies, a nemtabrutinib daily dose of 65 mg was selected as the monotherapy RP2D and the dose to be investigated in phase 3 monotherapy studies. In BELLWAVE‐003, CLL/SLL participants treated with 65 mg nemtabrutinib have shown an objective response rate of 35.0% with a median follow‐up of 9.1 months. Nemtabrutinib 45 mg showed similar efficacy; in contrast, no PR or CRs were observed in participants treated with ≤ 30 mg nemtabrutinib. While a dose of 80 mg was initially explored in BELLWAVE‐003, higher rates of treatment‐emergent AEs and more severe AEs were experienced by patients at this dose, which is no longer under development. The 65 and 45 mg doses have demonstrated a manageable and tolerable safety profile.

Our preliminary exposure‐response efficacy analysis, based on BELLWAVE‐001 and BELLWAVE‐003 pooled CLL/SLL patient data showed a significant trend of increased probability of BOR with exposure to nemtabrutinib; doses below 45 mg were predicted to be less efficacious than higher doses. Preliminary expsoure‐response analysis for safety, based on pooled data across indications, showed a significant trend between exposure and increased probability of any‐grade drug‐related AE (as assessed by investigator) and any‐grade hypertension. However, no significant trend was found for Grade ≥ 3 events, other safety events of concern listed above, or tolerability endpoints (dose discontinuations, reductions, modifications).

Overall, our preliminary expsoure‐response analyses support an improved benefit‐risk profile at 65 mg compared to lower or higher doses. The models will be further updated to include data from ongoing phase 3 studies, in which extensive safety and efficacy data, including progression free survival, will be accrued. Further analysis, including data from Phase 3 studies in previously untreated patients, will explore patient‐specific disease characteristics which may impact prognosis, such as prior treatment with BTKi/BCL2 inhibitors and tumor suppressor p53 TP53 gene aberrations [22].
